chapter: Arriving in New York and Mingus
title: Sitting in with Mingus: 'Cherokee' and 'Stormy Weather'
summary: Mingus grills the kid with the tuba from the bandstand, tests him on a blues, 'Cherokee' and 'Stormy Weather', and hires him.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: But Red Callender taught Mingus to play the bass. And so he was kind of angry and grumpy and everything else. And Jaki Byard, they were just about to take the stand and Jaki Byard said, “There’s your tuba player over there.” And Mingus, “You mean that kid?” Now at this point in the gig or whatever was going on, Mingus always called his band the Jazz Workshop. That gave him a chance to use anything you know. He could stop a band and rehearse a section that they didn’t get so well. He could change the key or change the meter. Because it was the Jazz Workshop, right?
Oh so he used that as a —

So when he spoke to the band from the bandstand, I mean, he almost always said into the microphone, so he pulled up the mic and he says, “You mean that kid back there? “Yeah, he’s got a tuba but can he play it?” And Jaki didn’t want to get too involved because he didn’t know my playing. So he said, “I don’t know, why don’t you ask him?” And Mingus looked at me and said, “You play behind the beat like most tuba players?” I said, “No, I haven’t been told that.” So he said, “What tunes do you know?” Now at this point the audience was looking between Mingus and me wondering what’s going on. Because they’d never seen people do that on the bandstand. Mingus said, “What tunes do you know?” I didn’t understand the question, because I knew the tunes I needed to know to get along in New York. I was ready to play on whatever you called. Because that’s what I thought a jazz musician did, not seek dispensation for it being a difficult instrument you know. It’s like I actually heard a guy do that and he was kind of fumbling all over himself and I tried to mention that without trying to bust him. He says, “Hey man, it’s a tuba, what do you want?”

No, no. So, because I didn’t understand Mingus’ question, I said, “What tunes do you want to hear?” The audience went, “Woooooh.” A challenge being hurled. “Oh you’re bad. Are you bad enough for that? Come on up here and we’re going to see about this.” So that’s what I did. I went and played some blues tune or other. And the audience was cheering. And he said, “On that blues you were doubled up pretty fast on a couple of choruses. You couldn’t play an uptempo tune, could you?” I said, “Yeah, I’m sure I can.” So he called “Cherokee” you know, the big challenging fast tune. I had to run a couple of choruses of that. And the audience again was on the underdog’s side. So Mingus said, “Okay we’re playing Birdland the next five days” or something like that, opposite the Coltrane quartet. I was like, “Yeah, baby.” So the first rehearsal is tomorrow afternoon here at the Five Spot. And the audience was going, “Yeah, yeah, yeah.” They didn’t stop. So he said, “I’d like to hear you play a ballad.” It was under the auspices of the Jazz Workshop. So he asked me to play “Stormy Weather.” And at some point in the tune things got a little strange. Each time we got to a certain point it got a little strange. And © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

he said, “Okay, you’ve still got the gig but learn how to play ‘Stormy Weather’ right.” So I went, “Well what was wrong with it?” He said, “You know the part that says, ‘It’s raining all the time/it’s raining all the time.’ You have to say that two times.”
He wanted you to tag it.
So I’m like, “Okay, you still win.” I mean I wasn’t trying to make it that but it got to be that.
